title: The Laughing Song
version_notes: Preferred historical transfer selected; exact recording date/version still to verify
notes: George Washington Johnson (1846–1914), pioneering African American recording artist and widely described as the first African American phonograph recording star. Supporting sources: http://www.library.ucsb.edu/OBJID/Cylinder17216 ; https://digitalcollections.nypl.org/items/5c9be900-c58f-012f-35fb-58d385a7bc34 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Johnson_(singer). Period marketing used overtly racist language, including 'the original whistling coon and laughing darkey'; retain this wording only as documented historical context, not as present-day description.

title: The Whistling Coon
version_notes: Preferred historical transfer selected; exact recording date/version still to verify
notes: Johnson's other signature recording. Lyrics are explicitly racist and dehumanising; retain the track because this repertoire is central evidence of the racial caricature embedded in the early commercial recording business. Supporting sources: https://genius.com/George-w-johnson-the-whistling-coon-lyrics ; https://www.npr.org/transcripts/5224572

title: Twinkle, Twinkle Little Star
version_notes: Early Berliner disc performance; exact date/catalogue details still to verify
notes: Technological artefact from the emergence of the lateral-cut gramophone disc. Supporting sources: https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/LordsPrayer_TwinkleTwinkleLittleStar.pdf ; https://www.clpgs.org.uk/concert-no7---berliner-5-discs.html ; https://soundofthehound.com/2011/05/20/emile-berliner-cuts-the-first-discs-tvinkle-tvinkle-little-star-how-i-vunder-vot-you-are/ ; alternate YouTube transfer https://youtu.be/T61TYOVtF3Y. CLPGS notes a Berliner disc whose reverse label lists 'Heil Dir' and 'God Save the Queen', sharing the same tune — a neat reminder of the melody's German/British royal history.
